analysis.one_liner: Requires 100% renewable electricity by 2035 and zero US emissions by 2050.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final two days of the session, the bill drew no cosponsors, never left committee, and died when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Energy to write rules so that 100% of US retail electricity comes from renewable sources by 2035, and set yearly energy-savings targets for electric and gas utilities. It also would have required the EPA to set annual emissions targets putting US greenhouse gas emissions 52% below 2005 levels by 2035 and at zero by 2050, with regulations to enforce them. It was introduced with two days left in the legislative year, got no cosponsors, and never received a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be everyone exposed to climate change — essentially everyone — through mandated cuts in the emissions driving wildfires, floods, and extreme heat, plus cleaner air from replacing fossil combustion. The bill's own findings argue efficiency mandates would save consumers money on energy bills. Renewable energy companies and efficiency contractors would gain a guaranteed, federally mandated market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone exposed to climate change; renewable energy firms

how_it_helps.text: Requires DOE to write rules so that 100% of electricity sold at retail in the US comes from renewable sources by 2035, with the share rising every year starting in 2022.

Requires the EPA to set annual net emissions targets so US greenhouse gas emissions in 2035 are at least 52% below 2005 levels and reach zero by 2050, with final enforcement regulations due within seven years of enactment.

Sets cumulative electricity- and natural-gas-savings targets for utilities through 2030, achieved through efficiency improvements at customer facilities, which the bill's findings describe as saving consumers money; suppliers could trade credits in a market-based system to lower compliance costs.

Requires a National Academies review every five years of whether the targets are sufficient, with a mechanism forcing agencies to act on (or formally explain declining) the Academies' recommendations.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers would lose their market as the electricity supply must be fully renewable by 2035. Electric and gas utilities would bear the cost of meeting the renewable and efficiency mandates, and some of those costs would likely be passed to households and businesses through rates during the transition. The bill provides no money for any of this — no transition aid for fossil fuel workers or communities and no direct subsidies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers, utilities, and ratepayers

drawbacks.text: Requiring 100% renewable electricity by 2035 — roughly a dozen years after introduction — is an extremely aggressive deadline that would demand a massive rebuild of the grid; compliance costs would likely show up in electric bills, and the bill contains no provisions to ease that transition for consumers.

The bill offers no transition assistance for fossil fuel workers or the communities that depend on those jobs and tax revenue, and includes no funding provisions at all — every obligation is a mandate enforced by regulation.
It delegates enormous discretion to DOE and EPA rulemaking — the entire program's real-world shape would be set by unelected agency regulators, subject to later revision every five years.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors, including none from the sponsor's own party, suggesting even allies viewed it as not ready for serious consideration.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goals track mainstream climate science — the bill's findings cite the IPCC and National Climate Assessment on the risks of exceeding 1.5–2°C of warming — and efficiency standards can genuinely lower energy bills over time. But the design is blunt: a hard 100%-renewable deadline with no consumer-transition funding, no help for displaced fossil fuel workers, and no cost containment beyond a credit-trading system for efficiency. Even a supporter would acknowledge the near-term price and grid-reliability risks of the timeline, and the total reliance on agency rulemaking makes the outcome dependent on future administrations.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last two days of the legislative year, sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its environment subcommittee, and sat there until Congress went out of session — no hearing, no vote, no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Lieu introduced the bill on December 30, 2021, with two days remaining in the first session of the 117th Congress.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the same day and to that committee's Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change the next day, December 31, 2021.
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The action record shows no further activity — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, which kills all unpassed bills.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and electric and gas utilities are better off, because the zero-emissions mandate they would have faced never came. No household gained or lost anything, since the bill never came close to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel producers (coal, oil, natural gas)
industries.note: The bill's zero-emissions mandate — 100% renewable electricity by 2035 and net-zero US emissions by 2050 — would phase out the market for their products. Their interest in stopping it ran directly against the bill's climate and clean-air benefits for the public.

Utilities would bear heavy obligations: converting to fully renewable supply by 2035 and hitting cumulative efficiency targets, though a credit-trading system would soften compliance costs. Costs would likely be passed to ratepayers, while cleaner power benefits the public.
A federal mandate forcing all retail electricity to be renewable by 2035 would guarantee enormous demand for wind, solar, and storage. This aligns with the public's interest in decarbonization.
Retail natural gas suppliers would face binding cumulative savings targets rising to 4.05% by 2030, reducing sales of their product. Consumers would save on gas bills as a result.
